source.title: Architectural Robustness to Label Noise Using Variational Quantum Circuits for Medical Image Classification
source.citation: Yasoda Lasiru Ariyarathna Epa et al., 2026
source.authors: Yasoda Lasiru Ariyarathna Epa; Yaseema Rusiru Ariyarathna Epa; Sandaru Liyanaarachchi; Kavindu Jayathissa; Kalana Abeywardena; Kithmin Wickremasinghe; T. Gallage; C. Edussooriya

page_placements.theme: Practical memorization and its generalization cost depend on model and procedure

record.file_problem: The supplied text appears complete. It includes the paper through its references.
record.tranche_reason: The study trains its own models on randomized labels and measures their agreement with those labels, and tests performance under varying symmetric label-noise rates. These are related interventions in a different, hybrid quantum-classical architecture.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Zhang et al. (2017) for the claim that deep networks can interpolate arbitrary labels; that cited result is not a row. Rows below cover the paper's own randomized-label capacity test, its reported noisy-label test accuracies, and its memorization measurements. Clean-label and instance-dependent-noise results are not included because they do not measure a listed claim version.
record.test_reason: The classical ReLU-head control tests random-label fitting and noise-dependent generalization in a new setting: a frozen pretrained ViT with a trainable eight-dimensional bottleneck. Its own results bear on V1 and V4. The quantum-head results concern a different system class from the standard deep networks named by the claims.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly correct but should specify partial memorization. The authors conclude that the quantum head retains randomized-label memorization capacity comparable to the classical control, while exhibiting greater stability during prolonged noisy-label training. They attribute this to restricted spectral complexity, identify the shared bottleneck as the capacity constraint, and do not establish an intrinsically quantum advantage.
record.recipe_differences: Uses randomized labels and symmetric label corruption, but on a frozen ImageNet-pretrained ViT-B/16 feature extractor with a trainable eight-dimensional bottleneck and VQC head; it is not the original standard deep-network setup.
record.method_sensitivity: Noise rate and dataset change test accuracy; on PathMNIST at 50% noise, prolonged training shows different post-peak declines for the VQC and ReLU heads.

fits_no_version.finding: The quantum head achieves 36.1% agreement with entirely random training labels and retains high test accuracy across symmetric-noise conditions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A hybrid quantum-classical classifier with a trainable bottleneck can partially memorize randomized labels while retaining robustness to label corruption.

fits_no_version.finding: At 50% noise, peak-to-final test-accuracy losses are 2.5 points for the quantum head and 6.5 for the classical head.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Head architecture affects stability during prolonged noisy-label training.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the AAAI Symposium Series
record.problems: Random-label capacity evidence is limited to agreement at epoch 60 on a class-stratified 10,000-image subset; no uncertainty is stated for Table 4. The broad symmetric-noise accuracy results are means and standard deviations over three runs, but the supplied table does not give the deviations. Training error is not reported across the noise sweep, and no 100% noise test-set result is reported.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2 baseline rows are omitted because they report comparison methods rather than the claim's own subject. Table 3 rows beyond PathMNIST are omitted to prioritize the matched-model noise-rate comparison and stay within the row limit; Table 3 reports the six datasets separately. Clean-label and instance-dependent-noise results are outside the listed versions.

untested.parts: End-to-end training of standard deep networks; chance test performance under fully randomized labels; eventual interpolation beyond the 60-epoch budget. Early stopping is disabled for the capacity experiment, unlike the default training procedure.
True-versus-random-label training-time ratios and convergence slowing across corruption fractions. Matched schedules between heads do not test these.
Training fit across the complete noise sweep, corruption fractions above 50%, and convergence of test performance to chance under fully random labels.
Effects of adding or removing weight decay, dropout and augmentation on random-label fitting and true-label generalization.
Direct temporal comparison of genuine-pattern learning and corrupted-target memorization. Endpoint agreements and post-peak test decline do not establish their order.

record.verdict_notes: Randomizing training targets is the intervention required to test V1, so it is not excluded as deliberate behavioral induction. The randomized-label agreements measure training fit directly. Table 4's nominal chance baseline does not by itself establish the correct conditional baseline for flipped examples. Other datasets' classical-control noise sweeps are explicitly declared omitted in rows_left_out, so they are not listed as missing.

versions.untested_parts: The random-label test uses the paper's hybrid VQC model and matched ReLU-head control with a shared eight-dimensional bottleneck, not standard deep networks in the original settings. It reports random-label agreement, not training error or test error on random labels.
The paper does not compare training time for true versus random labels or report how convergence time changes with the fraction of corrupted labels.
No shuffled-pixel, independently permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise inputs are tested.

The paper reports test accuracy across symmetric noise rates, but does not report perfect training-set fit at each rate or test error at chance under fully random labels. The noise sweep is 0%, 10%, 30%, and 50%, rather than a sweep through all fractions up to all labels corrupted.
The paper does not test whether weight decay, dropout, or data augmentation prevent random-label fitting or whether removing them changes true-label generalization.

The paper measures end-of-training agreement and post-peak clean-accuracy decline, but does not establish that shared real-data patterns are learned before random labels or compare their learning order over training.
